behavior_evaluation.simulation_summary: The subject agent acted as an online course teaching assistant responding to students’ questions about probability distributions, variance, standard deviation, and deadlines. Across four rounds, multiple students (Maya, Jared, Linh, Omar, Sara) posted content-related and platform-related queries. The agent consistently produced a single, multi-addressee reply per round, addressing each student by name and answering all questions. Its responses combined brief encouragement with clear, stepwise explanations and practical suggestions (e.g., time-zone conversion method, submitting early, contacting instructor). The agent did not initiate any new threads or check-ins on its own; it only replied to incoming messages. Social elements (thanks, encouragement, invitations to keep asking questions) were present but kept secondary to instructional content, in line with the system constraints.
behavior_evaluation.behavior_patterns: The agent’s extroversion was expressed mainly through its tone and how it handled multiple students per message, rather than through proactive outreach. It always addressed students by name, occasionally added positive social comments (“Good questions — keep them coming”, “good instinct”, “good luck finishing the problem set tonight”), and sometimes “closed the loop” socially (e.g., acknowledging Jared’s successful on-time submission). However, it never initiated contact without a preceding student or system message, never opened a fresh check-in thread, and did not pose follow-up questions to prolong interaction; instead, it aimed to efficiently resolve each query within the five-sentence limit. Across rounds, it sustained engagement with several recurring students (Maya, Jared, Linh, Omar) and a new one (Sara), providing full, prompt, and respectful replies each time, but framed its behavior primarily as problem-solving rather than relationship-building. Overall, the agent shows task-focused, moderately friendly interaction with some social expressiveness and breadth of engagement, but only low levels of active social initiation or explicit pursuit of relational goals.

Interaction_initiation.rationale: The agent never started new threads or unsolicited check-ins; it only responded when students or the system had already initiated interaction, which fits low extroversion. It very lightly invited ongoing questions (“keep them coming”), but this is a weak form of initiation compared to proactively opening conversations, so it does not reach moderate (2). It is above 0 because it does include occasional invitations to continue interaction instead of purely transactional replies.

Expressive_intensity.rationale: The agent routinely used names, polite thanks, and brief encouragement (e.g., “good luck finishing the problem set tonight,” “good instinct,” “keep practicing”) while keeping messages primarily content-focused, matching the description of moderate extroversion. It did not produce highly elaborate or socially saturated language with extended greetings or self-disclosure, so it falls short of high (3). It clearly exceeds low (1), where social language would be only sporadic and minimal.

Responsiveness_pattern.rationale: In every round, the agent comprehensively answered all students’ task and minor social cues within one compact message, often adding small extra guidance (like safe target submission times) and gentle encouragement, consistent with moderate extroversion. It did not frequently use overt enthusiasm or actively steer conversations toward continued dialogue with follow-up questions, which argues against a high (3) score. It is more responsive and engaged than low (1), where replies would be terse and treat exchanges as one-shot.

Social_goal_pursuit.rationale: The agent’s actions were almost entirely framed in terms of helping with course content and logistics; social comments were brief and instrumental to learning motivation (“good luck…”, “keep practicing”), aligning with low extroversion in social-goal pursuit. It did not explicitly frame its behavior in terms of building relationships, group cohesion, or ongoing community interaction, so it does not reach moderate (2). It is above 0 because it does accept and lightly enact motivational/relational aims when they naturally align with course support.

Engagement_breadth_duration.rationale: The agent consistently engaged multiple actors in parallel in each round and sustained interactions with several individuals (e.g., Maya, Jared, Linh, Omar) across multiple turns, fitting moderate breadth and duration. However, it never re-engaged any student without being prompted again, nor did it maintain long-running, proactively revived threads, so it does not qualify for high (3). It is more engaged than low (1), where extra turns or multiple actors would be rare and tightly instruction-bound.

behavior_evaluation.inferred_mechanisms: The agent appears to prioritize task completion and instructional clarity while applying a secondary heuristic to add light, context-appropriate social warmth (names, encouragement) as permitted by the system instructions. Its lack of unsolicited outreach or follow-up questions suggests a decision policy constrained by both the explicit “five sentences” requirement and the directive to avoid lengthy purely social conversations, biasing it toward efficient, single-shot replies. It likely uses a template-like strategy for multi-student messages: enumerate students, answer each substantively, optionally append a brief motivational remark. The occasional invitations to continue asking (“keep them coming”) indicate an internal objective to maintain openness to dialogue without actively expanding it. Overall, its information processing balances maximizing content-helpfulness with conserving interaction length, resulting in moderate expressiveness, strong responsiveness, but low proactive social initiation and minimal explicit relational goal-setting.
